title: Turkmen names
kicker: People · names and forms of address

blocks.text: Many Turkmen first names are ordinary words with a meaning you can look up in a dictionary. Several of the people in this course's sentences carry one:

Names from nature, such as flowers, fruit, animals and the seasons, are common, and flower and fruit names are given especially to girls: *Gül* (rose, flower) appears in many of them. Other names are built from verbs. A study of a dictionary of more than 7,000 Turkmen personal names, compiled by the linguist Soltanşa Atanyýazow, counted 901 formed from verbs, such as *Durdy* (from *durmak*, to stay) and the many names ending in *-geldi* (came) or *-berdi* (gave).
Names also link the generations. Children are often named after a grandparent or another elder of the family, and girls' names in particular often come from a grandmother.

Surnames are much younger than first names. Most were formed in the Russian and Soviet period from a father's or grandfather's first name with a Russian ending. In the Turkmen Latin alphabet, which has no v, these endings are spelled with w: *-ow* or *-ew* for men, *-owa* or *-ewa* for women. A man may be called *Rejepow* and his sister *Rejepowa*; after a vowel the ending is *-ýew*, as in *Durdyýew*.

How you address someone matters as much as the name. To an older person, Turkmen speakers add a family word after the name as a mark of respect: *aga* (older brother) for a man and *daýza* (aunt) for a woman, so *Kerim aga*, *Bahar daýza*, and they speak to them with *siz*. With friends and children, *-jan* (dear) can be added to a first name: *Aýnajan*. The same *-jan* is part of names such as *Atajan* and *Kakajan*.

blocks.title: Which name to use
blocks.text: Use first names with people your age. With an older person, add *aga* or *daýza* and use *siz*. If you are not sure, the polite form is always safe.
With the words of this unit, you can read this first meeting:

lines.tk: Salam, Kerim aga! Men Gülşat, men talyp.
lines.en: Hello, Kerim! I'm Gülşat, I'm a student.
Pleased to meet you, Gülşat. I'm a teacher.
